title: Federal Criminal Procedure Under the FRCrimP Rules
description: Pre-charge investigation and grand jury -> criminal complaint or indictment -> arrest, initial appearance, and detention/bail determination -> arraignment and pretrial release -> Rule 12 pretrial motions (defective indictment, suppression, Speedy Trial Act) -> Rule 16 and Brady/Giglio discovery -> Rule 11 plea negotiations and the change-of-plea colloquy -> trial (Rule 29 acquittal motions, jury verdict) -> post-trial motions and U.S.S.G. sentencing -> Rule 35 correction, the FRAP 4(b) notice-of-appeal window, and direct appeal. Citations checked against the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, Title 18, the Sentencing Guidelines, and the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure. Walk mode teaches the Rule 12(c)(3) pretrial-motions waiver trap, the jurisdictional (Bowles v. Russell) character of the FRAP 4(b) notice-of-appeal deadline, and the unextendable 14-day Rule 29(c)/33/35(a) post-verdict clocks.
jurisdiction: Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure / U.S. District Courts

nodes.label: Pre-Charge Investigation
nodes.note: Search warrants (Rule 41) require probable cause before a magistrate judge. The five-year statute of limitations in 18 U.S.C. § 3282 applies to non-capital federal offenses, measured from the offense date, not from discovery of the crime — a trap when investigating old conduct.

nodes.label: Grand Jury Convened
nodes.note: Grand jury proceedings are sealed under Rule 6(e); the target has no right to have counsel present in the jury room. Probable cause is the standard, not proof beyond a reasonable doubt, so hearsay and comparatively weak evidence suffice.

nodes.label: Grand Jury Votes
nodes.note: At least 12 of the 16-23 jurors must concur to return a true bill. If fewer than 12 concur, the foreperson must report the lack of concurrence to the magistrate judge in writing — the indictment is not effective.

nodes.label: Indictment Returned (True Bill)
nodes.cite: Fed. R. Crim. P. 6(f), 7; U.S. Const. amend. V
nodes.note: The Fifth Amendment requires grand jury indictment for federal felonies unless waived. The indictment must be returned in open court by the foreperson and starts the Speedy Trial Act clock together with arraignment (18 U.S.C. § 3161(c)(1)).

nodes.label: No Bill — Grand Jury Declines to Indict
nodes.cite: Fed. R. Crim. P. 6(f); Blockburger v. United States, 284 U.S. 299 (1932)
nodes.note: Double jeopardy does not attach at the grand jury stage, so the government may re-present the same charges to a different grand jury. Jeopardy attaches only when the trial jury is sworn (or the first witness is sworn in a bench trial). PLACEHOLDER PAYOFF: $1,000,000, override per matter, treating this playthrough's dispositive outcome as a full win even though double jeopardy has not yet attached and the government could theoretically re-present (not modeled as a loop back in this playthrough's payoff).

nodes.label: Criminal Complaint Filed
nodes.note: Sworn written statement of essential facts administered under oath before a magistrate judge. A separate probable-cause affidavit is typically attached; the complaint itself need only allege the essential elements of the offense.

nodes.label: Arrest / Warrant or Summons Executed
nodes.note: Defendant must be brought before a magistrate 'without unnecessary delay' — the McNabb-Mallory rule, now codified at 18 U.S.C. § 3501(c). Violation is not itself unconstitutional but triggers suppression of statements as the remedy; there is no bright-line federal day count.

nodes.label: Initial Appearance
nodes.note: Magistrate advises the defendant of the charges and rights and appoints or confirms counsel. TRAP: many defendants unknowingly waive the preliminary hearing right at this stage — an invalid waiver requires the court to hold the hearing anyway.

nodes.label: Preliminary Hearing
nodes.note: Only available if not yet indicted; the magistrate applies a probable-cause standard and hearsay is permitted. Automatically moot if the grand jury indicts before the hearing concludes (Rule 5.1(f)) — the government can bypass an unfavorable PC ruling by indicting first.

nodes.label: Bound Over to Grand Jury
nodes.note: The magistrate's probable-cause finding binds only the magistrate's own determination — the grand jury retains independent power to decline indictment, reduce charges, or indict on different counts entirely.

nodes.label: Complaint Dismissed — No Probable Cause
nodes.note: Magistrate finds no probable cause; defendant discharged on this complaint. Not a double jeopardy bar — jeopardy has not attached, so the government routinely re-prosecutes via grand jury indictment on the same conduct. PLACEHOLDER PAYOFF: $800,000, override per matter. Slightly discounted from a full win because, per this terminal's own note, the government 'routinely re-prosecutes via grand jury indictment' on the same conduct.

nodes.label: Detention Hearing (Bail Determination)
nodes.note: Bail Reform Act factors: flight risk, danger to the community, and the nature/severity of the charges. A rebuttable presumption of detention applies to certain violent-felony and serious drug offenses under § 3142(e)(3), shifting the burden to the defendant; the court must state its reasons in writing.

nodes.label: Released on Bail/Conditions
nodes.note: Conditions can include personal recognizance, bail, travel restrictions, curfew, GPS monitoring, house arrest, or a third-party custodian. Violating conditions triggers revocation proceedings under § 3142(g) and may result in detention.

nodes.label: Detained Pending Trial
nodes.note: Detained defendants receive priority under the Speedy Trial Act's 70-day trial clock. Defendant may move at any time to reopen detention based on newly discovered evidence; the court must hold a hearing within three days absent waiver.

nodes.label: Information Filed
nodes.note: Available as of right for misdemeanors; for felonies, requires a knowing and voluntary waiver of indictment in open court or in writing. Proceeding on an information starts the Speedy Trial Act clock like an indictment does.

nodes.label: Arraignment
nodes.note: Defendant is informed of the charging instrument in open court and enters a plea. Arraignment is the later of the two trigger dates (with indictment/information) for the Speedy Trial Act's unextendable 70-day trial clock.

nodes.label: Not Guilty Plea Entered
nodes.note: Default plea when no agreement yet exists. Does not preclude simultaneous or later plea negotiations — the case proceeds into pretrial motions and discovery while plea talks may run in parallel.

nodes.label: Rule 12(c) Motions Deadline Set
nodes.note: Court sets the Rule 12(b)(3) motion deadline at arraignment or as soon thereafter as practicable; if no deadline is set, all pretrial motions are due at trial's start. This deadline triggers the Rule 12(c)(3) waiver trap below.

nodes.label: Pretrial Motions Window
nodes.note: Motions that MUST be raised before trial include a defective indictment, suppression of evidence, severance, and Speedy Trial Act violations. Failure to raise these by the deadline forfeits them unless good cause is shown — most claims cannot be revived on appeal.

nodes.label: Motion to Dismiss Indictment Filed
nodes.note: Common grounds: a defective indictment (fails to state an offense), duplicity, multiplicity, statute-of-limitations expiration, and grand jury selection defects. Dismissal may be with or without prejudice depending on the defect's nature.

nodes.label: Motion to Suppress Evidence Filed
nodes.cite: Fed. R. Crim. P. 12(b)(3)(C); U.S. Const. amend. IV
nodes.note: Challenges evidence from a warrantless search/seizure or an involuntary statement (Miranda/Fifth Amendment). If granted, the government loses the evidence; if denied, the ruling is automatically preserved for direct appeal under the 2014 Rule 12(b)(3) amendment.

nodes.label: Suppression Motion Granted
nodes.cite: Fed. R. Crim. P. 12(d); Mapp v. Ohio, 367 U.S. 643 (1961)
nodes.note: Excluded evidence often cripples the prosecution; the government may instead take an interlocutory appeal under 18 U.S.C. § 3731 to preserve the ruling for review, or proceed without the suppressed evidence if the case is still viable.

nodes.label: Suppression Motion Denied
nodes.note: Denial is automatically preserved for direct appeal without renewing the objection at trial under the 2014 amendment — the defendant need not re-object during trial to preserve the issue.

nodes.label: Indictment Dismissed — Defective/Time-Barred
nodes.note: May be with or without prejudice. Dismissal without prejudice is only truly final if the five-year limitations period (18 U.S.C. § 3282) has since run — otherwise re-indictment remains possible. PLACEHOLDER PAYOFF: $700,000, override per matter. Discounted because, per this terminal's own note, dismissal without prejudice leaves re-indictment possible until the five-year limitations period runs.

nodes.label: Rule 12(c) Waiver — Motion Forfeited
nodes.cite: Fed. R. Crim. P. 12(c)(3); Davis v. United States, 411 U.S. 233 (1973)
nodes.note: TRAP. An untimely Rule 12(b)(3) motion is forfeited absent a showing of good cause for the delay — a flexible but demanding standard. Most defenses are lost for good, though a narrower plain-error path can survive for some suppression claims on direct appeal. PLACEHOLDER PAYOFF: $100,000, override per matter. Not itself a verdict -- the defense loses its best pretrial motion, and the case proceeds toward an assumed unfavorable trial posture in this playthrough.

nodes.label: Dismissed — Speedy Trial Act Violation
nodes.note: 70-day trial-start clock from indictment or first appearance, whichever is later, minus excludable delay under § 3161(h). Dismissal under § 3162(a)(2) can be with or without prejudice based on offense seriousness and the impact on Speedy Trial Act administration. PLACEHOLDER PAYOFF: $900,000, override per matter.

nodes.label: Rule 16 Discovery Exchange
nodes.note: Government must disclose the defendant's statements, prior record, documents/objects, and expert reports — only upon the defendant's request. Reciprocal defense discovery is triggered once the defendant requests. Distinct from Brady/Giglio, which apply regardless of request.

nodes.label: Brady/Giglio Disclosure
nodes.cite: Brady v. Maryland, 373 U.S. 83 (1963); Giglio v. United States, 405 U.S. 150 (1972)
nodes.note: A continuing constitutional obligation, not a discretionary discovery rule: prosecutors must disclose evidence favorable to the accused material to guilt or punishment (Brady), including impeachment evidence such as witness deals (Giglio). No fixed deadline, and no limitations period bars post-conviction relief for a violation.

nodes.label: Discovery Dispute / Motion to Compel
nodes.note: Defendant may move to compel when the government fails to produce Rule 16 discovery. The court has broad discretion under 16(d) to order compliance, grant a continuance, or fashion any other just remedy; Brady disputes follow the same framework.

nodes.label: Discovery Sanction Imposed
nodes.note: Sanctions range from a continuance (least severe) to exclusion of evidence to dismissal of charges. Brady/Giglio violations are especially treacherous: suppression can support post-conviction relief years later, so prevention is the only reliable remedy.

nodes.label: Plea Negotiations
nodes.note: Prosecutors and defense counsel may discuss dispositions outside court; the court cannot participate. Three agreement types: (A) charge bargain, (B) non-binding sentencing recommendation, (C) binding specific sentence or range. Absent a written or on-the-record agreement, this is negotiation only.

nodes.label: Plea Agreement Reached
nodes.note: Must be disclosed in open court at the plea hearing unless the court allows in-camera disclosure for good cause. A Rule 11(c)(1)(C) binding-sentence agreement gives the defendant a statutory right to withdraw the plea if the court rejects the agreed disposition (Rule 11(c)(5)).

nodes.label: Change-of-Plea Hearing (Rule 11 Colloquy)
nodes.note: Court must address the defendant personally, ensure the plea is knowing and voluntary, confirm understanding of the rights waived and the penalties (including any mandatory minimum), and establish a factual basis. A defective colloquy is a frequent ground for appellate reversal.

nodes.label: Guilty Plea Accepted
nodes.note: Before accepting any guilty plea, the court must establish a factual basis sufficient to support each element of the offense — a bare admission alone is insufficient. Once accepted, the case bypasses trial entirely and proceeds straight to the presentence report.

nodes.label: Plea Rejected by Court
nodes.note: Court may reject a (B)-type non-binding recommendation or a (C)-type binding agreement it deems unwarranted or contrary to law. Rejecting a binding agreement under (c)(5) entitles the defendant to withdraw the plea; rejecting a non-binding recommendation does not.

nodes.label: No Plea Agreement — Proceed to Trial
nodes.note: Negotiations failed or the defendant declined to plead; the Speedy Trial Act clock (18 U.S.C. § 3161, typically 70 days from indictment/arraignment) continues to run toward trial preparation, including pretrial motions, discovery, and jury selection.

nodes.label: Jury Selection (Voir Dire)
nodes.note: Peremptory and for-cause challenges are available; a Batson v. Kentucky challenge polices race- or gender-based peremptory strikes through a prima facie case, a race-neutral explanation, and a totality-of-circumstances review.

nodes.label: Trial in Progress
nodes.note: Government presents its case-in-chief first and must prove every element beyond a reasonable doubt; the defense has no constitutional obligation to present a case at all under the Fifth Amendment.

nodes.label: Rule 29 Motion for Judgment of Acquittal
nodes.cite: Fed. R. Crim. P. 29(a), (c); Jackson v. Virginia, 443 U.S. 307 (1979)
nodes.note: Standard is whether any rational trier of fact could find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, viewing the evidence most favorably to the government. May be made mid-trial (29(a)) or renewed after verdict within 14 days (29(c)); double jeopardy consequences differ sharply by timing.

nodes.label: Judgment of Acquittal — Rule 29 Granted
nodes.note: Government's evidence was legally insufficient. Double jeopardy bars a government appeal of a pre-verdict Rule 29(a) grant; a post-verdict Rule 29(c) grant CAN be appealed because a guilty verdict already existed before the court set it aside. PLACEHOLDER PAYOFF: $1,000,000, override per matter.

nodes.label: Rule 29 Motion Denied
nodes.note: Case proceeds to the jury. Defense need not renew the motion at the close of all evidence to preserve the right to renew it after verdict under Rule 29(c).

nodes.label: Mistrial — Hung Jury
nodes.cite: Fed. R. Crim. P. 26.3; Arizona v. Washington, 434 U.S. 497 (1978)
nodes.note: A genuinely hung jury is manifest necessity for a mistrial. Double jeopardy does NOT bar retrial after a hung jury, unlike after an acquittal — jeopardy attached but was never terminated.

nodes.label: Case Dismissed After Hung Jury
nodes.note: Government exercises prosecutorial discretion not to retry, with leave of court. Unlike an acquittal, double jeopardy did not compel this outcome — the government could have retried but chose not to. PLACEHOLDER PAYOFF: $1,000,000, override per matter.

nodes.label: Verdict Returned
nodes.note: Verdict must be unanimous in federal court (Rule 31(a)); either party may request that the jury be polled (Rule 31(d)), and the court may declare a mistrial if the poll reveals a lack of unanimity.

nodes.label: Acquittal by Jury Verdict
nodes.cite: Fed. R. Crim. P. 31(a); U.S. Const. amend. V
nodes.note: Double jeopardy permanently bars retrial or a government appeal on this charge, no matter how erroneous the verdict looks on the law or the facts. PLACEHOLDER PAYOFF: $1,000,000, override per matter.

nodes.label: Guilty Verdict
nodes.note: Conviction on the merits; the defendant may renew the Rule 29 acquittal motion or move for a new trial before sentencing — the two motions carry distinct deadlines from one another.

nodes.label: Rule 33 Motion for New Trial
nodes.note: General grounds carry a strict 14-day post-verdict deadline, but a newly-discovered-evidence claim gets up to 3 years — a trap because the evidence must have been genuinely unavailable at trial, not merely overlooked or reconsidered.

nodes.label: Presentence Investigation Report (PSR)
nodes.note: Probation must prepare and disclose the PSR at least 35 days before sentencing (waivable). Both parties may object to factual findings and Guidelines calculations before the hearing.

nodes.label: Sentencing Hearing
nodes.note: Defendant has an absolute right of allocution. The court must correctly calculate the Guidelines range as a starting point (Gall/Booker framework) even though the range is now advisory and the court may vary from it for policy reasons.

nodes.label: Guidelines Range Calculated
nodes.note: Base offense level, adjusted for specific offense characteristics and aggravating/mitigating factors, crossed with Criminal History Category on the Sentencing Table, yields the advisory range — mandatory to calculate even if the final sentence deviates from it.

nodes.label: Departure/Variance Considered
nodes.cite: U.S.S.G. § 5K1.1; 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a); United States v. Booker, 543 U.S. 220 (2005)
nodes.note: A 'departure' is Guidelines-authorized (e.g., a government-only § 5K1.1 substantial-assistance motion); a 'variance' is a discretionary deviation under the § 3553(a) factors post-Booker. Both must be explained on the record.

nodes.label: Judgment and Commitment Entered
nodes.note: Written judgment is the appealable final disposition; it simultaneously starts the Rule 35(a) 14-day correction clock and the FRAP 4(b) 14-day appeal clock. Modeled as terminal because it is reached identically whether the conviction came by plea or by jury verdict, even though Rule 35/appeal paths still branch from it. PLACEHOLDER PAYOFF: $50,000, override per matter. A conviction (by plea or verdict); modeled as terminal here even though Rule 35/appeal paths still branch from it in the pack's own edges (see this node's note).

nodes.label: Rule 35 Motion to Correct/Reduce Sentence
nodes.note: Rule 35(a) lets the court correct clear error (arithmetic, technical, procedural) within 14 days of sentencing — not a substantive do-over. Rule 35(b) lets the government move to reduce a sentence for post-sentencing substantial assistance within one year, with no effect on this 14-day window.

nodes.label: Notice of Appeal Window
nodes.note: Defendant has 14 days from judgment entry to file. The district court may extend up to 30 additional days for excusable neglect or good cause — but only if the extension motion is itself made within the original 14-day window. Post-Bowles, this is jurisdictional with no equitable exceptions.

nodes.label: Notice of Appeal Filed
nodes.note: A timely notice of appeal meeting FRAP 3's form requirements and FRAP 4(b)'s deadline is the jurisdictional invocation of appellate review. Notice must be filed in the district court; premature or delayed filings do not cure jurisdictional defects.

nodes.label: Appeal Forfeited — FRAP 4(b) Deadline Missed
nodes.cite: Fed. R. App. P. 4(b); Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007)
nodes.note: TRAP. The deadline is absolute and jurisdictional. Bowles held that even a district court's own miscalculation and invitation to file late does not excuse a missed window. Only 28 U.S.C. § 2255 collateral review — a far harder standard — remains. PLACEHOLDER PAYOFF: $0, override per matter. Conviction stands and appellate review is forfeited by a missed deadline, not by choice -- worse than a deliberate waiver.

nodes.label: Conviction Final — No Appeal Taken
nodes.note: Defendant deliberately lets the window lapse, often pursuant to an appeal-waiver plea agreement. Judgment becomes final for purposes of the AEDPA collateral-review clock under 28 U.S.C. § 2255(f); direct appeal is no longer available. PLACEHOLDER PAYOFF: $100,000, override per matter. Per this terminal's own note, this is often reached 'pursuant to an appeal-waiver plea agreement' -- a deliberate, negotiated finality, valued slightly above an unreviewed trial conviction.

nodes.label: Appellate Briefing
nodes.note: Standard of review varies by issue — de novo for legal questions, clear error for factual findings, abuse of discretion for sentencing procedure and most evidentiary rulings. Failure to raise an issue in the brief forecloses it on appeal.

nodes.label: Court of Appeals Decision
nodes.note: Panel may affirm, reverse and render, reverse and remand for a new trial, or vacate and remand for resentencing only — a common partial win limited to the sentencing package.

nodes.label: Conviction Affirmed on Appeal
nodes.note: Judgment is final. Further review is discretionary: en banc rehearing (rarely granted), certiorari to the Supreme Court (rarer still), or a 28 U.S.C. § 2255 collateral attack limited to constitutional/jurisdictional error or newly available structural defects. PLACEHOLDER PAYOFF: $0, override per matter.

nodes.label: Conviction Reversed / Remanded
nodes.cite: 28 U.S.C. § 2106; Burks v. United States, 437 U.S. 1 (1978)
nodes.note: Court of appeals can remand for a new trial, for resentencing only, or with instructions to dismiss. Under Burks, reversal for evidentiary insufficiency bars retrial like an acquittal; reversal for trial error (instructional, evidentiary, Brady) permits retrial.
